name: Opus 5 event driven
strategy: A concentrated hard-catalyst book anchored on the contested Brighthouse takeover, with the CRH/Arcosa cash spread as low-beta carry, a live Hormuz supply-disruption energy leg, and the macro index short retired.
reassessment_note: BASELINE WRITE - refining. Three changes. (1) Cut ACA from 26% to 11%: at 146.50 against an approved $150 cash deal the gross spread is 2.39% to a Q1-2027 close, roughly cash-plus-3% annualized, while a break takes the stock to the low 100s. That is the wrong risk/reward for the book's largest weight. (2) Upsize BHF from 11% to 32%: Delaware is grilling Aquarian on its sources of capital, the Sept 6 outside date already slipped to a hard Dec 6, and Talcott/Sixth Street has reaffirmed in writing that it will take the company if Aquarian fails. That makes $50 a price with a rival-bid floor underneath it and $70 above it. (3) Close the 8% SPY short: the Fed hiked to 3.75-4% on Sept 16 and signalled another, and the index went up anyway. The leg has cost money, pays 3% borrow, and an index short does not hedge idiosyncratic deal-break risk.

positions.thesis: The book's best asymmetry and now its anchor. BHF closed 10-02 at 50.02 against Aquarian's signed $70 all-cash merger; stockholders approved and every condition except Delaware, New York and Massachusetts insurance approvals is satisfied or waived. The spread is wide because Delaware's regulator questioned founder Rudy Sahay behind closed doors about where Aquarian's capital is coming from, and the Sept 6 outside date auto-extended to a hard Dec 6. The reason to be long at 50 is the floor, not the spread: Talcott Financial, backed by Sixth Street, sent the board a private letter reaffirming it wants the company if Aquarian falls through, after a reported $55 approach. So the realistic outcomes are $70 on a close, mid-50s on a Talcott takeout, and mid-40s only if both fail - a distribution with most of its mass above today's price. The 36% take-profit sits just under $70 so a deal close is banked at the print rather than left to a delisting; the 22% stop is deliberately wide because selling the gap on a break is exactly wrong when a funded rival bidder is waiting.

Trimmed from 17% but kept, as the one live non-deal catalyst and the book's only inflation hedge. Brent settled near $99.68 and WTI near $91.24 on 10-02 with Hormuz traffic still far below pre-war levels and the US weighing a second carrier into the region, so the supply-disruption premium is intact and unresolved. Expressing it through XLE keeps the exposure in producers - XOM, CVX and COP are 48% of the fund - rather than refiners whose cracks compress on crude spikes. Trimmed rather than held flat because the leg has already paid: XLE is up 44.6% over twelve months and sits within 5% of its 52-week high of 66.17, so a credible ceasefire headline is a fast drawdown. Hence the tighter 10% stop against the prior 12%.

Kept as low-beta carry but cut to a size the spread actually justifies. Arcosa stockholders approved CRH's $150 all-cash acquisition on Sept 4; only regulatory clearance is outstanding and the close is guided to Q1 2027. At 146.50 that is a 2.39% gross spread over roughly four months - around 7% annualized against 4% on cash, so the genuine excess return is thin, which is why this is 11% and not 26%. What it still earns its place for is correlation: a shareholder-approved cash deal does not care what the Fed does in October, which is worth holding alongside a 32% position whose own risk is regulatory. The real risk is aggregates overlap drawing a DOJ second request, and the 8% stop only triggers on an actual break, not on spread noise.
